technique.how: Curvilinear probe, patient supine. Trace the aorta in transverse from the xiphoid (celiac/SMA level) to the bifurcation, measuring outer-wall-to-outer-wall diameter at proximal, mid and distal segments, then confirm in long axis. Any segment >3.0 cm is an aneurysm; use graded compression to displace bowel gas.
technique.prerequisites: Trained operator; visualization of the entire infrarenal aorta to the bifurcation; measure outer to outer wall, perpendicular to the vessel.
technique.contraindications: None; do not delay resuscitation or surgical consult in unstable patients to complete the scan.

interpretation.positive_finding: Aorta >3 cm on ED POCUS is essentially diagnostic of AAA (pooled specificity 98%); in a symptomatic or hypotensive patient this is a presumed rupture until proven otherwise.
interpretation.negative_finding: A complete scan showing aorta <3 cm along its full length effectively excludes AAA (pooled sensitivity 99%, LR- ~0.01); it does not exclude dissection or retroperitoneal bleed from other causes.
interpretation.pitfalls: POCUS cannot reliably detect rupture itself (retroperitoneal blood is often not seen); an incomplete scan due to bowel gas or obesity is non-diagnostic, not negative. Mistaking IVC or oblique cuts for aorta, and measuring inner wall, cause errors.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive with symptoms/hypotension: activate vascular surgery and OR/CT per stability; negative complete scan removes AAA and redirects workup (dissection, mesenteric ischemia, renal colic).

estimates.target_condition: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (>=3 cm aortic dilation)
estimates.population: Adults with suspected AAA, 7 studies, 655 patients; ED bedside US by emergency physicians
estimates.reference_standard: CT, MRI, aortography, radiology US, laparotomy or autopsy
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.99/(1-0.98); LR- = (1-0.99)/0.98 from pooled sens/spec in abstract
estimates.quote: sensitivity 99% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 96% to 100%) and specificity 98% (95% CI = 97% to 99%)

sources.citation: Rubano E, Mehta N, Caputo W, Paladino L, Sinert R. Systematic review: emergency department bedside ultrasonography for diagnosing suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acad Emerg Med. 2013;20(2):128-138.
Lederle FA, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Does this patient have abdominal aortic aneurysm? JAMA. 1999;281(1):77-82.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not treat an incomplete or technically limited scan as negative; do not use POCUS to exclude rupture or to exclude aortic dissection.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: AAA >3 cm with pain, syncope or hypotension: immediate vascular surgery call, large-bore access, blood products, and OR or CT depending on stability.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Included studies used variably trained emergency physicians after brief courses; pooled accuracy was consistently excellent across all 7 studies, but indeterminate scans were handled inconsistently.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Emergency physician with basic POCUS training (course plus supervised scans) obtaining a complete transverse sweep of the infrarenal aorta; indeterminate studies must be counted as non-diagnostic.

extraction_notes: Pooled sens/spec and the weighted prevalence (23% in symptomatic patients >50) are from the Rubano 2013 abstract; LRs computed from those values without CIs. Full text is not open access, so per-study tables were not inspected. Lederle 1999 RCE cited as the index/contrast for physical exam accuracy.
